pages.x: The Falklands, windswept islands in the South Atlantic, had been British since 1833 and were home to about 1,800 people, most of them of British descent. Argentina, 500 kilometres away, has always claimed them as Las Malvinas. In 1982 its military rulers, facing anger over a failing economy and the thousands of people they had made disappear, decided to take them.

On 2 April 1982 Argentine troops landed near Stanley, the capital, and after a short fight the small garrison of Royal Marines surrendered. Huge crowds in Buenos Aires cheered General Galtieri, the head of the junta. He did not believe Britain would fight for islands so far away.

Britain's prime minister, Margaret Thatcher, decided to fight. Within days a task force set sail, two small aircraft carriers leading more than a hundred ships, among them cruise liners turned into troopships, on a voyage of 13,000 kilometres. Talks to find a peace on the way all failed.

On 2 May a British submarine sank the Argentine cruiser General Belgrano, and 323 of its crew died, almost half of all the Argentines killed in the war. Two days later an Argentine jet hit the destroyer HMS Sheffield with an Exocet missile, and it later sank. Argentine pilots, flying low over the waves, went on to sink five more British ships.

On 21 May British troops landed at San Carlos, on the far side of East Falkland from Stanley. Most of their big helicopters had gone down with the ship carrying them, so they crossed the island on foot, carrying huge loads over bog and rock: the marines called it yomping. They won at Goose Green, then took the hills around Stanley in night battles.

On 14 June, with British troops on the edge of Stanley, the Argentine garrison surrendered, after 74 days of war. Many of the Argentine dead were young conscripts, cold and hungry in their foxholes. Three islanders, all women, were killed by a British shell.

Defeat brought down Argentina's junta, and democracy returned there in 1983. Victory made Thatcher hugely popular, and she won the next election by a landslide. Argentina still claims the islands; in a vote in 2013 all but three of the islanders who voted chose to stay British.
pts: Britain won the islands back in 74 days
Defeat brought democracy back to Argentina
